translations.text: that the man to whom things fall out most pleasantly on earth does not know how I, wretched and full of care, spent the winter on the ice-cold sea on the paths of exile, cut off from my dear kinsmen, hung about with icicles; hail flew in showers.
The shadow of night grew dark, snow came from the north, frost bound the ground, hail fell on the earth, the coldest of grains.

And so the thoughts of my heart now press on me to try for myself the high streams, the tossing of the salt waves. Again and again my mind's desire urges my spirit to set out, so that far from here I may seek the land of foreigners.
And so for every man the praise of the living who speak of him afterward is the best memorial: that before he must go on his way he should work, by good deeds on earth against the malice of fiends,
by brave deeds against the devil, so that the children of men may praise him afterward, and his praise may then live with the angels for ever and ever, the glory of eternal life, joy among the hosts.

The days are gone, and all the pomp of the kingdom of earth. There are now no kings or emperors or gold-givers such as there once were, when they did the greatest glorious deeds among themselves and lived in the most lordly renown.
This whole noble company has fallen, and the joys are gone. The weaker ones remain and hold this world, and enjoy it through toil.
Glory is brought low. The nobility of the earth grows old and withers, as every man now does throughout the world.
